examples.ko: 남자 친구는 군필이라서 복학 걱정이 없어요.
examples.en: My boyfriend has finished his military service, so he has no worries about returning to school.

examples.ko: 이 회사는 군필 지원자를 우대한다고 들었어요.
examples.en: I heard this company gives preference to applicants who have completed military service.

examples.ko: 저는 군필이고 동생은 아직 입대 전이에요.
examples.en: I have finished my service, and my younger brother hasn't enlisted yet.

examples.ko: 군필 여부를 이력서에 꼭 써야 해요?
examples.en: Do I have to write whether I've done military service on my résumé?
It's a program only people who have completed military service can apply for.

examples.ko: 친구들은 대부분 군필이어서 군대 이야기를 자주 해요.
examples.en: Most of my friends have finished their service, so they often talk about the army.

explain: 반대말은 '미필'이고, 사람을 가리킬 때는 '군필자'라고 해요. 이력서나 채용 공고에서 많이 보이고, 대화에서는 '군대 다녀왔어요'라고도 말해요.
explain_en: The opposite is '미필' (not yet served), and for a person you say '군필자'. It shows up on résumés and job postings, while in conversation people also say '군대 다녀왔어요' (I've been to the army).

examples.en: It rained, so my boots got completely soaked.

examples.ko: 아버지는 군대에서 신던 군화를 아직 갖고 계세요.
examples.en: My father still has the boots he wore in the army.

examples.ko: 새 군화는 처음에 발이 많이 아파요.
examples.en: New combat boots hurt your feet a lot at first.
I tied my boot laces tightly and set off.

examples.ko: 그 가수는 무대에서 검은 군화를 신고 나왔어요.
examples.en: The singer came out on stage in black combat boots.
I bought boots that look like combat boots on purpose.

explain: 군인이 신는 신발이지만 패션으로 신는 투박한 부츠를 가리킬 때도 있어요. 그런 부츠는 '워커'라고도 많이 불러요.
explain_en: It refers to the shoes soldiers wear, but it can also describe chunky boots worn as fashion. People also call that style '워커'.

examples.ko: 두 사람의 우정은 시간이 지나도 굳건해요.
examples.en: The two people's friendship stays firm even as time passes.

examples.ko: 그는 어려움 속에서도 굳건한 의지를 보여 줬어요.
examples.en: He showed unshakable willpower even in hard times.
Our team's trust was still firm.

examples.ko: 굳건하게 버티면 좋은 날이 올 거예요.
examples.en: If you hold on firmly, good days will come.

examples.ko: 마음이 굳건하지 않으면 금방 포기하게 돼요.
examples.en: If your mind isn't firm, you end up giving up quickly.

examples.ko: 두 나라의 관계는 여전히 굳건하다고 해요.
examples.en: They say the relationship between the two countries is still solid.

explain: 믿음, 우정, 의지, 관계처럼 쉽게 흔들리지 않는 것에 잘 어울려요. '굳건히'처럼 부사로도 많이 쓰고, 반대 느낌으로는 '흔들리다'를 써요.
explain_en: It fits things that don't waver easily, such as trust, friendship, will and relationships. It's also used as the adverb '굳건히', and the opposite idea is expressed with '흔들리다' (to waver).

examples.ko: 그 아이는 몸은 작아도 마음이 굳세요.
examples.en: That child is small, but strong in spirit.
With a steadfast will, I ran to the end and finished the race.

examples.ko: 어머니는 힘든 일이 있어도 굳세게 버티셨어요.
examples.en: My mother held on steadfastly even through hard times.

examples.ko: 큰 꿈을 이루려면 마음이 굳세어야 해요.
examples.en: To achieve a big dream, your heart has to be strong.
The players stayed steadfast to the end even while losing.
I was ashamed of myself for not being strong.

explain: 주로 사람의 마음, 의지, 태도가 흔들리지 않고 강할 때 써요. 힘이 센 것을 말하는 '세다'와 달리 몸의 힘보다 마음에 초점이 있어요. '굳세게 살아라'처럼 격려하는 말로도 써요.
explain_en: It is mostly used for a person's heart, will or attitude that stays strong. Unlike '세다' (strong), the focus is on mental strength, not body strength. It also appears in encouragement like '굳세게 살아라'.

examples.ko: 기타를 오래 쳐서 손가락에 굳은살이 생겼어요.
examples.en: I played guitar for a long time, so calluses formed on my fingers.

examples.ko: 발뒤꿈치 굳은살을 없애려고 따뜻한 물에 담갔어요.
examples.en: I soaked my feet in warm water to get rid of the calluses on my heels.

examples.ko: 일을 많이 하신 아버지의 손은 굳은살투성이예요.
examples.en: My father's hands, which have worked a lot, are full of calluses.

examples.ko: 굳은살은 너무 두꺼워지면 아플 수 있어요.
examples.en: Calluses can hurt if they get too thick.
What soft hands, without any calluses.

examples.ko: 매일 연습한 사람만 이런 굳은살을 가질 수 있어요.
examples.en: Only someone who practices every day can get calluses like these.

explain: '굳은살이 생기다', '굳은살이 박이다'처럼 말해요. 오래 연습하거나 일한 흔적이라서 '손에 굳은살이 박였어요' 하면 노력했다는 느낌도 있어요. 가운데에 단단한 심이 있는 '티눈'과는 달라요.
explain_en: You say '굳은살이 생기다' or '굳은살이 박이다'. Because it's a trace of long practice or work, '손에 굳은살이 박였어요' can also suggest hard effort. It differs from '티눈' (a corn), which has a hard core.

examples.ko: 가고 싶은 마음은 굴뚝같지만 일이 많아요.
examples.en: I badly want to go, but I have a lot of work.

examples.ko: 지금 당장 먹고 싶은 마음이 굴뚝같아요.
examples.en: I'm dying to eat it right now.

examples.ko: 쉬고 싶은 마음이 굴뚝같았지만 참고 일했어요.
examples.en: I longed to rest, but I held back and kept working.

examples.ko: 도와주고 싶은 마음은 굴뚝같은데 방법이 없어요.
examples.en: I really want to help, but there's no way.

examples.ko: 여행 가고 싶은 생각이 굴뚝같아서 표를 알아봤어요.
examples.en: I was so eager to travel that I looked up tickets.

examples.ko: 그만두고 싶은 마음이 굴뚝같다고 친구가 말했어요.
examples.en: My friend said he is desperate to quit.

explain: 거의 '~고 싶은 마음이 굴뚝같다' 모양으로만 써요. 바라는 마음은 아주 큰데 현실은 그렇게 못 할 때 '굴뚝같지만'이라고 말하는 경우가 많아요.
explain_en: It is used almost only in the form '~고 싶은 마음이 굴뚝같다'. People often say '굴뚝같지만' when the wish is huge but reality doesn't allow it.

examples.en: The ball rolled down the hill.
I tumbled down the stairs and hurt my arm.
It's dangerous if stones roll down from the mountain.
The child almost rolled off the bed.
I saw an apple roll out of the box and fall.
Be careful not to tumble down from a high place.

explain: '떨어지다'는 그냥 아래로 내려오는 것이고, 굴러떨어지다는 구르면서 떨어지는 모습까지 보여 줘요. 사람이 계단에서 넘어져 구르는 상황에도 써요.
explain_en: '떨어지다' just means to fall down, while 굴러떨어지다 also shows the rolling motion on the way. It's also used for a person who trips and tumbles down stairs.

examples.en: A soccer ball suddenly rolled to my feet.
A coin rolled over from over there, so I picked it up.
What if a huge rock comes rolling down on the mountain path?

examples.ko: 아이가 던진 공이 굴러오는 걸 잡았어요.
examples.en: I caught the ball the child threw as it rolled toward me.

examples.ko: 이 구슬은 도대체 어디서 굴러온 거예요?
examples.en: Where on earth did this marble roll in from?

examples.ko: 공이 굴러오지 않아서 직접 가지러 갔어요.
examples.en: The ball didn't roll back, so I went to get it myself.

explain: 말하는 사람 쪽으로 구르면서 다가오는 것을 말해요. 반대로 멀어지면 '굴러가다'를 써요. '굴러온 돌'처럼 비유로 쓰는 말도 있어요.

phrases.example: 새로 온 직원이 오래 일한 선배보다 인정받았어요. 굴러온 돌이 박힌 돌 빼낸다더니 딱 그 모양이에요.
phrases.en: The new employee got more recognition than the senior who worked there for years. It's just like the saying 'the rolled-in stone pushes out the embedded stone.'
phrases.nuance_ko: 나중에 들어온 사람이 원래 있던 사람의 자리를 차지할 때 쓰는 속담이에요. 밀려난 쪽의 서운함이 담겨 있어요.
phrases.nuance_en: A proverb for when a newcomer takes the place of someone who was there first. It carries the hurt feelings of the person pushed out.
phrases.en_equiv: the newcomer pushes out the old-timer

explain_en: It describes something rolling toward the speaker. When it moves away, you use '굴러가다'. There is also a figurative use like '굴러온 돌'.

examples.en: That actor has a deep, thick voice, which is impressive.
The wooden pillar looks thick and sturdy.
Big, thick raindrops started to fall.
Please write the letters in bold, thick strokes.
These potatoes are really big and thick.

examples.ko: 그 형은 어릴 때부터 팔뚝이 굵직했어요.
examples.en: That older guy has had thick forearms since he was little.

explain: '굵다'보다 꽤 굵고 듬직한 느낌이에요. 목소리나 선, 나무에 쓰고, '굵직한 사건'처럼 크고 중요한 일을 말할 때도 써요.
explain_en: Compared with '굵다', it feels solidly thick and dependable. It's used for voices, lines and trees, and also for big, important matters, as in '굵직한 사건'.

examples.ko: 강아지를 하루 종일 굶기면 안 돼요.
examples.en: You must not leave a puppy without food all day.
No parent lets their child go hungry.
I was busy yesterday and left my cat without food.
No matter how angry you are, don't make your child go hungry.
I didn't mean to make my little brother go hungry.

examples.ko: 벌로 밥을 굶기는 건 좋은 교육이 아니에요.
examples.en: Making a child skip meals as punishment is not good parenting.

explain: '굶다'는 내가 먹지 않는 것이고, 굶기다는 다른 사람이나 동물을 먹지 못하게 하는 거예요. '밥을 굶다'와 '아이를 굶기다'를 구분해서 써요.
explain_en: '굶다' is when you yourself go without eating, while 굶기다 means making another person or animal go without food. Compare '밥을 굶다' with '아이를 굶기다'.

examples.en: The corruption of the ruling class was on the news.

examples.ko: 권력층과 가까운 사람들이 특혜를 받았다고 해요.
examples.en: They say people close to those in power received special favors.

examples.ko: 일반 시민은 권력층을 쉽게 만나기 어려워요.
examples.en: It's hard for ordinary citizens to meet the people in power.
Those in power must be equal before the law too.
In the novel, the powerful class torments weak people.
He tried hard to get into the circle of power.

explain: 정치나 경제의 힘을 쥔 사람들을 묶어서 말해요. 돈과 지위가 높은 '상류층'과 겹치지만 초점은 힘, 곧 권력에 있어요. 뉴스나 신문에서 자주 나오는 말이에요.
explain_en: It groups together people who hold political or economic power. It overlaps with '상류층' (upper class), which focuses on wealth and status, but 권력층 focuses on power. It is common in news and newspapers.

examples.ko: 책 권수가 너무 많아서 책장이 모자라요.
examples.en: I have so many books that my bookshelf is too small.

examples.ko: 한 사람이 빌릴 수 있는 권수는 다섯 권이에요.
examples.en: The number of books one person can borrow is five.
With a complete set, check the number of volumes first before buying.

examples.ko: 권수로 따지면 제가 더 많이 읽었어요.
examples.en: In terms of the number of books, I've read more.
The library has a limit on the number of books you can borrow.
I didn't know how many volumes the series had, so I asked at the bookstore.

explain: 책을 셀 때 쓰는 '권'에 '수'가 붙은 말이에요. 같은 책이 몇 개 있는지 세는 '부수'와는 달라서, 서로 다른 책이나 한 시리즈의 권이 몇 개인지를 말할 때 써요.
explain_en: It combines '권', the counter for books, with '수' (number). It differs from '부수' (number of copies); 권수 is about how many volumes, whether different books or parts of one series.

en: period of boredom (esp. in a relationship); slump

examples.en: In our third year of marriage, we hit a slump.
How did you two get through your slump?
When a couple enters a slump, their conversations get fewer.
Maybe I'm in a rut lately, because I don't want to do anything.

examples.ko: 권태기는 누구나 한 번쯤 겪는 것 같아요.
examples.en: I think everyone goes through a slump like this once.
I hear some people break up because of this stage.

explain: 연인이나 부부 사이에서 서로에게 싫증이 나는 시기를 많이 말해요. 일이나 취미에 흥미가 떨어졌을 때도 써요. 결과가 안 나오는 '슬럼프'와 달리 지루함과 싫증이 중심이에요.
explain_en: It's most often used for the stage when partners grow bored of each other, but also when you lose interest in work or a hobby. Unlike '슬럼프' (a performance slump), it centers on boredom and weariness.

examples.en: It suddenly poured on my way home.

examples.ko: 늦은 밤 혼자 걷는 귀갓길이 무서워요.
examples.en: The walk home alone late at night is scary.
The subway on the way home is always crowded.
The route home in front of the school has been made safe.
They patrol for the children's safe walk home.
Walking with a friend makes even the way home enjoyable.

explain: '퇴근길'은 일을 마치고, '하굣길'은 학교를 마치고 가는 길인데, 귀갓길은 어디서든 집으로 돌아가는 길이라 더 넓게 써요. 밤길 안전 이야기에서 특히 자주 들려요.
explain_en: '퇴근길' is the way home after work and '하굣길' after school, but 귀갓길 covers going home from anywhere. It is often heard in talk about safety on night streets.

examples.ko: 설 연휴 마지막 날 귀경길은 오후부터 정체가 시작돼요.
examples.en: On the last day of the Lunar New Year holiday, traffic back to Seoul starts building up in the afternoon.

examples.ko: 부모님이 챙겨 주신 반찬을 들고 귀경길에 올랐어요.
examples.en: I set off back to Seoul carrying the side dishes my parents packed.
Cars returning to Seoul have flooded in, so the highway is jammed.
So many people are returning to Seoul that the train tickets sold out.
The rest stop on the way back to Seoul was packed with people.

examples.ko: 연휴 마지막 날에는 귀경객들로 서울역이 북적여요.
examples.en: On the last day of the holiday, Seoul Station is crowded with people returning to Seoul.

explain: 명절에 고향에 갔다가 서울로 돌아오는 것을 말하고, 반대는 고향으로 가는 '귀성'이에요. 보통 '귀경길', '귀경 차량'처럼 뉴스에서 명절마다 들려요.
explain_en: It means returning to Seoul after visiting your hometown for a holiday, and the opposite is '귀성' (going to your hometown). It is usually heard in forms like '귀경길' and '귀경 차량' in holiday news.

en: holiday travelers heading to their hometowns

examples.en: Ahead of the Lunar New Year, people heading to their hometowns are flooding in.

examples.ko: 귀성객을 위해 임시 열차를 더 운행해요.
examples.en: They run extra trains for people going home for the holiday.
The terminal was crowded all day with holiday travelers going home.

examples.ko: 올해 귀성객은 작년보다 줄어들 것 같아요.
examples.en: This year's hometown-bound travelers will probably be fewer than last year.

examples.ko: 고속도로 휴게소에서 귀성객에게 차를 나눠 줬어요.
examples.en: They handed out tea to holiday travelers at the highway rest stop.
Most people heading to their hometowns leave early in the morning.

explain: 설이나 추석 같은 명절에 고향으로 가는 사람들을 말해요. 고향에서 돌아오는 사람은 '귀경객'이라고 해요. '귀성길', '귀성 전쟁'처럼 명절 뉴스에서 자주 나와요.
explain_en: It refers to people going to their hometowns for holidays such as Seollal or Chuseok. People returning from their hometowns are '귀경객'. It appears often in holiday news in phrases like '귀성길' and '귀성 전쟁'.

examples.en: That person has an uncannily sharp sense for reading situations.

examples.ko: 귀신같은 솜씨로 고장 난 시계를 고쳤어요.
examples.en: He fixed the broken watch with uncanny skill.
My younger brother's prediction for this exam was spooky accurate.
His judgment was so uncanny that everyone was amazed.
Isn't the timing of the arrival uncanny?
I visited a fortune-teller who is rumored to be uncannily accurate.

explain: 무서운 느낌이 아니라 어떻게 알았지 싶을 만큼 정확하거나 뛰어날 때 감탄하며 쓰는 말이에요. 눈치, 솜씨, 예측, 타이밍 같은 말과 자주 어울려요.
explain_en: It isn't about being scary. It's an exclamation for when someone is so accurate or skilled that you wonder how they knew. It often goes with words like 눈치, 솜씨, 예측 and 타이밍.

examples.en: My younger sibling guessed my password as if by magic.
Mom spots a lie in no time, like she has a sixth sense.
He shows up out of nowhere only when I'm hungry.
He solved the problem with uncanny speed.

examples.ko: 제가 지갑을 두고 온 걸 귀신같이 아셨네요.
examples.en: You figured out uncannily that I left my wallet behind.
My older brother found my weak spot uncannily fast.

explain: 귀신처럼 정확하고 빠르게 무언가를 알거나 해내는 모습을 말해요. '귀신같이 알다', '귀신같이 맞히다', '귀신같이 나타나다'를 자주 써요. 감탄이나 가벼운 놀림이 섞인 구어체예요.
explain_en: It describes knowing or doing something with uncanny accuracy and speed. Common pairings are '귀신같이 알다', '귀신같이 맞히다' and '귀신같이 나타나다'. It's colloquial, mixing admiration or light teasing.

examples.en: It's dangerous to dig deep into your ear with an ear pick.
Please find the ear pick in the drawer.
Ear picks are made of wood or metal.
I put an ear pick in my travel bag too.
If you don't have an ear pick, use a cotton swab.

examples.ko: 엄마의 귀이개에는 작은 솜털이 달려 있었어요.
examples.en: My mom's ear pick had a small tuft of fluff attached.

explain: '귀이개로 귀를 파다'라는 짝으로 많이 써요. 귀지를 파내는 작은 도구이고, 요즘은 면봉을 더 많이 쓰기도 해요.
explain_en: It is commonly paired as '귀이개로 귀를 파다' (to clean the ear with an ear pick). It's a small tool for removing earwax, though many people now use cotton swabs more.

examples.en: Please leave your valuables in the hotel safe.
I left my valuables behind when I got off, so I went back.
I put my bag in the valuables locker.

examples.ko: 귀중품이 든 가방은 항상 몸에 지니세요.
examples.en: Always keep the bag with your valuables on you.
There weren't even any valuables at home, but a thief broke in.
The more expensive the valuables, the more carefully you should store them.

explain: 현금, 보석, 중요한 서류처럼 잃어버리면 곤란한 물건을 묶어서 불러요. 호텔, 비행기, 사우나 같은 곳의 안내문에서 '귀중품은 직접 보관해 주세요'라는 말을 자주 봐요.
explain_en: It groups items that would be a problem to lose, such as cash, jewelry and important documents. You often see notices like '귀중품은 직접 보관해 주세요' at hotels, on planes and in saunas.

examples.ko: 귀지가 많이 쌓이면 잘 안 들릴 수 있어요.
examples.en: If a lot of earwax builds up, you may not be able to hear well.

examples.ko: 귀지를 너무 자주 파면 귀에 좋지 않아요.
examples.en: Digging out earwax too often isn't good for your ears.

examples.ko: 귀지는 사람에 따라 색이나 질감이 달라요.
examples.en: Earwax differs in color and texture from person to person.
My ear felt blocked because of earwax.
I heard earwax also plays a role in protecting the ear.
I asked the doctor about earwax.

explain: '귀지가 끼다', '귀지가 쌓이다', '귀지를 파다'처럼 말해요. 귀지를 파는 도구는 귀이개나 면봉이에요.
explain_en: You say '귀지가 끼다', '귀지가 쌓이다' and '귀지를 파다'. The tools for cleaning it are an ear pick (귀이개) or a cotton swab (면봉).

examples.en: I bumped my knee on the corner of the desk.
The corner of the picture frame is a little broken too.

examples.ko: 가게는 골목 귀퉁이를 돌면 바로 보여요.
examples.en: The shop is right there once you turn the corner of the alley.
A corner of the wall broke off.

examples.ko: 마음 한 귀퉁이는 늘 비어 있어요.
examples.en: One corner of my heart is always empty.
Only the corner of the book is slightly folded.

explain: 물건이나 땅이 모난 곳의 끝부분을 말해요. 방 안쪽처럼 안으로 들어간 곳은 '구석'이라고 더 자주 해요. '마음 한 귀퉁이'처럼 비유로도 써요.
explain_en: It refers to the tip or edge where an object or plot of land comes to a point. For an inner area like the inside of a room, '구석' is more common. It's also used figuratively, as in '마음 한 귀퉁이'.

en: beside the ear; by the ear

examples.en: The wind brushed past my ear.
That song is still ringing in my ears.
My ear tickled, so I turned around.
Someone whispered softly right by my ear.
I pushed the hair by my ear behind it.
I was so embarrassed that even my ears turned red.

explain: 귀의 바로 옆을 말해요. '귓가에 맴돌다'는 들었던 소리나 말이 계속 들리는 듯한 느낌일 때 자주 써요. 소설이나 노래 가사에서도 많이 나와요.
explain_en: It means the area right beside the ear. '귓가에 맴돌다' is often used when a sound or words you heard still seem to echo. It also appears a lot in novels and song lyrics.

examples.ko: 귓구멍에 물이 들어가서 잘 안 들려요.
examples.en: Water got in my ear, so I can't hear well.
After swimming, I wiped my ear canal opening clean.
It felt muffled, as if my ears were blocked.
Don't put a cotton swab all the way into your ear.

examples.ko: 아기 귓구멍은 아주 작아서 조심해야 해요.
examples.en: A baby's ear opening is very small, so you have to be careful.
The sound was so loud it rang deep in my ears.

explain: 귀 안쪽으로 들어가는 구멍을 말하지만, 일상에서는 그냥 '귀'라고 할 때가 많아요. '귓구멍이 막혔어?'처럼 말을 못 알아듣는 사람에게 핀잔을 주는 거친 말투로도 쓰니 조심하세요.
explain_en: It means the hole leading into the ear, but in daily talk people often just say '귀'. Be careful: '귓구멍이 막혔어?' is a rough way of scolding someone who doesn't listen.

examples.en: Earlobes quickly turn red when it's cold.
I put a small earring on my earlobe.
My mom fiddles with her earlobe when she's nervous.

examples.ko: 귓불이 두툼하면 복이 많다는 말이 있어요.
examples.en: There's a saying that thick earlobes mean good fortune.
The tip of my earlobe feels strangely itchy.
Please gently massage the earlobes too.

explain: 귀의 아래쪽에 말랑하게 늘어진 부분이에요. 귀걸이를 다는 곳이라 '귀걸이'와 함께 자주 나와요. 얼굴이 빨개질 때 '귓불까지 빨개졌다'고도 말해요.
explain_en: It's the soft hanging part at the bottom of the ear. Since it's where earrings go, it often appears with '귀걸이'. When someone blushes, people say '귓불까지 빨개졌다'.

examples.en: The child whispered a secret in her mom's ear.
Even whispering in the theater is surprisingly loud.
My friend whispered right into my ear.

examples.ko: 회의 중에는 옆 사람에게 귓속말하지 마세요.
examples.en: Don't whisper to the person next to you during the meeting.
What are you two whispering about like that?
I heard all of their whispering.

explain: '속삭이다'는 작은 소리로 말하는 것이고, 귓속말하다는 남이 못 듣게 상대 귀에 가까이 대고 말하는 거예요. '귓속말을 하다', '귓속말을 주고받다'처럼도 많이 써요.
explain_en: '속삭이다' means to speak in a low voice, while 귓속말하다 means putting your mouth near someone's ear so others can't hear. It's also common as '귓속말을 하다' or '귓속말을 주고받다'.

examples.ko: 그것참, 오늘따라 정말 신기한 일이 많네요.
examples.en: Well, what a lot of strange things happen today.
My, how did something like this happen?
Oh, what a pity. I have no words of comfort.

examples.ko: 그것참 큰일이네요. 어서 병원에 가 보세요.
examples.en: Oh dear, that's serious. Go to the hospital right away.
Well, that's odd. I'm sure I put it here.

examples.ko: 그것참, 아이가 말을 어쩜 이렇게 잘할까요?
examples.en: My goodness, how can a child speak so well?

explain: 뜻밖이거나 안타깝거나 어이없을 때 혼잣말처럼 내는 소리예요. 어떤 느낌인지는 말투에 따라 달라지고, 어른들이 많이 쓰는 말투예요. '허 참', '참 나'와 비슷하게 쓰여요.
explain_en: It's a murmur-like exclamation for when something is unexpected, sad or absurd. The feeling depends on your tone, and it's a typical adult way of speaking. It's used similarly to '허 참' and '참 나'.

examples.en: How are you lately? I'm getting by.
My salary is okay enough to get by on.
The food at that restaurant was so-so but okay.
I did so-so on this exam.

examples.ko: 그냥저냥 살다 보니 벌써 십 년이 지났어요.
examples.en: Just drifting along, ten years have already passed.
Work life is bearable, nothing special.

explain: 아주 좋지도 나쁘지도 않게 평범하다는 대답으로 자주 써요. '잘 지내요?'라는 인사에 '그냥저냥요'라고 답하기도 해요. 비슷한 말로 '그저 그래요'가 있어요.
explain_en: It is often used as a reply meaning neither very good nor bad, just ordinary. To a greeting like '잘 지내요?' people may answer '그냥저냥요'. A similar expression is '그저 그래요'.

examples.en: It's always shady under the tree, so it's cool.
Let's rest a bit in the shade before we go.

examples.ko: 건물 때문에 방이 일 년 내내 그늘져요.
examples.en: The room is shaded all year round because of the building.

examples.ko: 그늘지지 않은 자리를 찾아서 돗자리를 폈어요.
examples.en: I found a spot that wasn't shaded and spread out the mat.
The child's face looked gloomy, so I was worried.
If it's shaded, laundry doesn't dry well.

explain: 햇빛이 가려져 어두워진다는 뜻 외에, 표정이나 마음이 어두워 보일 때도 써요. 햇볕이 잘 드는 곳은 '양지바르다'라고 해요.
explain_en: Besides sunlight being blocked, it's also used when someone's expression or mood looks dark. A place that gets plenty of sunshine is called '양지바르다'.

examples.en: Anyway, what shall we eat tonight?
Anyway, when do the exam results come out?
By the way, are your parents doing well?

examples.ko: 그러나저러나 길이 막히는데 약속 시간에 맞출 수 있을까요?
examples.en: Anyway, the roads are jammed, so can we make it on time?

examples.ko: 일은 끝났어요. 그러나저러나 이제 집에 가요.
examples.en: The work is done. Anyhow, let's go home now.

examples.ko: 그러나저러나 우리 이번 주말에 만나는 거 맞죠?
examples.en: Anyhow, we're meeting this weekend, right?

explain: 앞 이야기가 어떻든 상관없이 화제를 바꾸거나 정말 중요한 이야기로 돌아올 때 써요. '그건 그렇고', '그나저나'와 비슷하게 쓰는 구어체예요.
explain_en: Use it to change the subject or return to what matters, regardless of what was said before. It's colloquial and works much like '그건 그렇고' and '그나저나'.

examples.en: His excuse was quite convincing.
I came up with a plausible excuse and skipped the appointment.
In the photo, the food looks decent.

examples.ko: 소문을 더 그럴듯하게 만들려고 숫자까지 지어낸 사람이 있었어요.
examples.en: Someone even made up numbers to make the rumor more believable.
There are many stories that sound plausible but aren't true.
In a hanbok, you look quite the part.

explain: 진짜처럼 믿을 만하거나 꽤 괜찮아 보일 때 써요. 말이 그럴듯하다고 하면 사실은 아닐 수도 있다는 의심이 살짝 들어가요. 반대로 '제법 그럴듯하네요'처럼 칭찬으로도 써요.
explain_en: Use it for something that seems believable or looks quite decent. Calling an account 그럴듯하다 can hint at slight doubt that it's actually true. It can also be praise, as in '제법 그럴듯하네요'.

examples.ko: 그 이야기는 듣다 보니 꽤 그럴싸해요.
examples.en: That story sounds quite plausible as I listen.
He gave a plausible reason, and I almost believed him.
After editing the photo, it came out looking quite convincing.
Don't be fooled by ads that look convincing.

examples.ko: 아이의 거짓말이 너무 그럴싸해서 웃음이 나왔어요.
examples.en: The child's lie was so convincing that I laughed.
It's a plausible-sounding plan, but difficult in practice.

explain: '그럴듯하다'와 거의 바꿔 쓸 수 있어요. 말이나 겉모습이 진짜 같아 보이지만 사실은 아닐 수도 있다는 느낌으로 자주 쓰여요.
explain_en: It can almost always be swapped with '그럴듯하다'. It is often used with the feeling that words or appearances look real but may not actually be.

examples.ko: 서울 외곽에는 그린벨트로 묶인 지역이 많아요.
examples.en: There are many areas on the outskirts of Seoul designated as greenbelt.

examples.ko: 그린벨트에서는 건물을 마음대로 지을 수 없어요.
examples.en: You can't build buildings freely in a greenbelt.
The government announced it would lift part of the greenbelt.

examples.ko: 그린벨트 덕분에 도시 주변에 숲이 남아 있어요.
examples.en: Thanks to the greenbelt, forests remain around the city.
If the greenbelt is lifted, will housing prices rise?
A walking trail has been built in the greenbelt in front of my house.

explain: 공식 이름은 '개발제한구역'이지만 뉴스와 일상에서는 '그린벨트'라고 더 많이 말해요. '그린벨트 해제'처럼 집값이나 부동산 이야기에서 자주 나와요.
explain_en: The official term is '개발제한구역', but in news and daily talk people more often say '그린벨트'. It often comes up in housing and real-estate talk, as in '그린벨트 해제'.

en: water colors; oil colors; tube colors

examples.en: I painted the sky blue with paints.
I ran out of paints, so I went to the art supply store.
I dipped my brush in paint mixed with water.

examples.ko: 아이가 그림물감 묻은 손으로 벽을 만졌어요.
examples.en: The child touched the wall with paint-covered hands.

examples.ko: 그림물감은 섞는 색에 따라 느낌이 달라져요.
examples.en: The feel of paints changes depending on the colors you mix.
Take the paints along with you too.

explain: 그림을 그릴 때 쓰는 물감을 말하는데, 일상에서는 그냥 '물감'이라고 하는 경우가 많아요. 종류는 '수채 물감', '유화 물감', '아크릴 물감'처럼 앞에 붙여서 구분해요.
explain_en: It means paint used for drawing or painting, but in daily speech people often just say '물감'. Types are distinguished by adding a word before it, such as '수채 물감', '유화 물감' and '아크릴 물감'.

en: be no more than that; be enough; That's it

examples.en: If you fail, you can just try again, and that's all.
The scenery here is the best, so I come often.
It wouldn't have mattered if he didn't come, but I waited.
On a hot day, cold noodles are just perfect.

examples.ko: 싫으면 안 가도 그만인데 왜 고민해요?
examples.en: If you don't like it, you can just skip it, so why worry?

examples.ko: 나만 괜찮으면 그만이라고 생각하면 안 돼요.
examples.en: You shouldn't think it's fine as long as it's fine for you.

explain: 두 가지로 써요. '~(으)면 그만이다'는 그걸로 끝이고 더 신경 쓸 게 없다는 뜻이고, '경치가 그만이다'는 아주 좋다는 뜻이에요. '그만두다'와 헷갈리지 말고, 앞의 쓰임은 무심하게 들릴 수 있어요.
explain_en: It has two uses: '~(으)면 그만이다' means that's all and nothing more needs worrying about, and '경치가 그만이다' means something is excellent. Don't confuse it with '그만두다' (to quit), and the first use can sound careless.

examples.en: It was last December. Around that time it snowed a lot.
Kids of that age love toys.
I was very short at that age too.
Around that time, flowers start to bloom.
Next March? By around then I'll have graduated too.
It was around that very time that I met my friend.

explain: 앞에서 말한 때나 나이 무렵을 가리켜요. 지금 이 무렵은 '이맘때'라고 하고, 같은 짝으로 '저맘때'도 있어요. '작년 이맘때'처럼 시기를 말할 때 자주 써요.
explain_en: It points to the time or age mentioned earlier. For the present time of year, use '이맘때', and there is also '저맘때' in the same set. It's often used for periods, as in '작년 이맘때'.

examples.en: The fishermen cast their nets into the sea.

examples.ko: 이 신발은 통풍이 잘 되는 그물망 소재예요.
examples.en: These shoes are made of breathable mesh material.
The roads are connected like a net.
A bird got caught in the netting.

examples.ko: 안전 그물망이 있어서 공이 밖으로 안 나가요.
examples.en: There's a safety net, so the ball doesn't go outside.
The welfare safety net needs to be woven more tightly.

explain: '그물'은 물고기를 잡는 도구 자체이고, 그물망은 그물처럼 얽힌 모양이나 구조까지 말해요. '복지 그물망'처럼 사회 제도를 비유할 때도 써요. 신발이나 옷의 '메쉬' 소재를 가리킬 때도 있어요.
explain_en: '그물' is the net tool itself, while 그물망 also covers net-like woven shapes and structures. It's used figuratively for systems, as in '복지 그물망' (welfare safety net). It can also refer to mesh material in shoes and clothes.

en: waning crescent moon (the moon at the end of the lunar month)

examples.en: A thin waning crescent moon hung in the sky at dawn.

examples.ko: 그믐달은 해가 뜨기 전에 잠깐 보여요.
examples.en: The waning crescent moon is visible briefly before sunrise.
I got up early to see the waning crescent moon.
After I trimmed my nail, it became thin like a waning crescent moon.
The waning crescent and the new crescent moon look alike.

examples.ko: 어제 새벽 그믐달에 조용히 소원을 빌었어요.
examples.en: Yesterday at dawn I quietly made a wish on the waning crescent moon.

explain: 음력 그믐 무렵에 새벽 동쪽 하늘에 뜨는 가는 달이에요. 모양이 비슷한 초승달은 저녁 서쪽 하늘에서 보여요. 시나 노래에서 쓸쓸한 분위기를 낼 때도 나와요.
explain_en: It's the thin moon that rises in the eastern sky before dawn near the end of the lunar month. The similar-looking crescent '초승달' appears in the western sky in the evening. It also appears in poems and songs to create a lonely mood.

en: be tanned; be scorched; be blackened (by sun, fire or smoke)

examples.en: After playing at the beach, my face got dark and tanned.
The wall was blackened with soot, so I repainted it.

examples.ko: 여름 내내 밖에서 일하면 피부가 그을어요.
examples.en: If you work outside all summer, your skin gets tanned.
Put on sunscreen so you don't tan too much.

examples.ko: 피부가 쉽게 그을 것 같아서 모자를 썼어요.
examples.en: I wore a hat because my skin seemed likely to tan easily.
I cleaned the pot that had been blackened by smoke.

explain: 햇볕을 받아 피부가 검게 되거나, 불과 연기 때문에 물건이 검게 변하는 것을 말해요. 피부는 일상 대화에서 '타다'라고 더 흔히 말해요. 연기나 불에서 생기는 검은 가루는 '그을음'이라고 해요.
explain_en: It describes skin darkening from the sun, or things turning black from fire and smoke. For skin, everyday talk more commonly uses '타다'. The black powder from smoke or fire is called '그을음' (soot).
